chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Sa'dan, from Mu'tab who said:

Abu Al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) was in his garden picking dates. I looked at one of his slaves who had taken a bunch of dates and threw it behind the wall. So I went to him, seized him, and brought him to the Imam. I said, 'May I be your ransom, I found this one and this bunch of dates.' He said to the slave, 'O So-and-so,' and he replied, 'At your service.' He asked, 'Are you hungry?' He said, 'No, my Master.' He asked, 'Are you naked (need clothes)?' He said, 'No, my Master.' He asked, 'Then for what reason did you take these?' He said, 'I desired that.' He said, 'Go, they are for you,' and he said, 'Leave him alone.'

key_terms.حَائِط: Garden or enclosed plot of land
key_terms.كَارَة: A bunch or cluster of dates
key_terms.لَبَّيْكَ: At your service / Here I am

ai.seo_question: How did Imam Musa al-Kazim (peace be upon him) handle a slave who took food without a specific need?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* highlights the pedagogical wisdom of Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS), who employed Socratic questioning to distinguish between mere caprice and genuine need before granting pardon. By asking 'Are you hungry?' and 'Are you naked?', he demonstrated that ethical correction requires understanding the root cause of behavior, a principle highly valued in Shia jurisprudence for distinguishing between minor faults and deserving of punishment. This narrative serves as a model for leaders and parents to prioritize mercy and insight over immediate retribution.

en.hubeali: A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Abu Abdullah, from Sa’dan, from Mo’tab who said,

‘It was so that Abu Al-Hassan Musa<sup>asws</sup> was by a (garden) wall of his<sup>asws</sup>, and he<sup>asws</sup> looked at a slave of his<sup>asws</sup> who had taken a bunch of dates, and he threw it behind the wall. So I went over to him, and seized it and went with him to him<sup>asws</sup>, and I said, ‘May I be sacrificed for you<sup>asws</sup>! I found this one that this bunch (of dates)’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said to the slave: ‘O so and so!’ He said, ‘At your<sup>asws</sup> service!’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Are you hungry?’ He said, ‘Yes, my Master<sup>asws</sup>!’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘So are you bare (need clothes)?’ He said, ‘Yes, my Master<sup>asws</sup>!’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘So, for which thing (reason) did you take these?’ He said, ‘I desired that’. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Go, for these are for you’. And he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Leave him alone’.
en.sarwar: 7. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn abu ‘Abd Allah from Sa’dan from Mu’attib who has said the following:

“Abu al-Hassan Musa (a.s.) once was in his compound that had palm-trees. 1 looked at one of his slaves who had picked up a certain amount of dates. He threw it on the other side of the wall. I went and picked up what he had thrown and I brought it to the Imam. I said, ‘May Allah keep my soul in service for your cause, 1 found him and this amount of dates.’ The Imam called the slave, ‘O so and so.’ ‘Yes, sir,’ the slave replied. ‘Are you hungry?’ asked the Imam. ‘No, sir,’ replied the slave. ‘Do you need clothes?’ asked the Imam. ‘No, sir,’ replied the slave. ‘What for did then you take this many dates?’ inquired the Imam. ‘I just wanted,’ said the slave. ‘Take them. They are for you. Let him go,’ the Imam said to others.’”
